checks: Compactness gives finitely many nonempty integer fibers. The finite union dimension is their maximum affine dimension, and Hausdorff q-measure is positive and finite on precisely the q-dimensional fibers. Their disjoint Borel union gives M as the stated sum.

A same-parity pair has integral midpoint. Fixing one summand gives a q-dimensional scaled translate contained in the midpoint fiber, so its dimension is exactly q and the midpoint belongs to P. The finite-set witness lemma then forbids two sites of any one parity in a P-empty vertex set.

The actual strict complement of a closed halfspace is open and convex, and intersection with C is bounded Borel and convex. For two bases in E_J the interpolated section contains the Minkowski average. If one section has dimension above q, a fixed point of the other gives a high-dimensional scaled translate. If both are q-dimensional with different direction spaces, relative open neighborhoods sum to a relatively open subset of their higher-dimensional direction sum. In either case H_q is infinite, exceeding the finite threshold.

For two q-sections with the same direction space, translate to that Euclidean q-space. Ordinary Brunn–Minkowski for measurable convex sections gives a strict root bound above the average threshold, which is at least ell at the interpolated site by convexity. This establishes E_J convex in every case.

The local premise excludes each z∈P from at least one E_J. Helly selects at most k of the sets, even though they can be nonclosed. The union of their actual original index sets has size at most kt. Its residual is included in a successful selected residual at every positive base, giving both the pointwise and summed bound.

For B≥0, subadditivity gives covered mass ≤ktB, while its complementary residual gives the required lower bound. If the allowance is at most (1−tg)M, division by kt gives B≥gM/k. At t=2, the d=1 and d=2 allowances evaluate to zero and M/9.
